Assessing the credibility of the claim means putting it into perspective, which in turn means you need reliable data for TOTAL deaths. Also, I recommend working with monthly data so you have lower relative variance; likewise, 60 seconds is a terrible interval, so I would scale up the claim to be 86400/month (or 2880/day if you go with data for daily total deaths).

Once you have data for total monthly deaths, trace a line which spans back from some years ago -- perhaps 5 to 10 years -- up until November 2020.

Then to test a claim about corona deaths, plot it as a single data point (or a line if you have an ongoing claim / ongoing updates from the same source). If it exceeds the total deaths then it is obvious bullshit, otherwise you can see what proportion of total deaths are being claimed as corona deaths.

Now invoke those previous years of data for total deaths, and calculate two things:

* Present total divided by past total (e.g. Nov 2020 / Nov 2019) -- call this ratio T

* Present corona divided by past total -- call this ratio C

If the claim is legit, you should have C = T-1 (approximately). This should also hold for 2020 vs 2019, 2020 vs 2018, etc.

If C < T-1 (significantly) then either the claim is an understatement, far more people are dying of other causes (potentially a new unidentified threat), or somewhere in between.

If C > T-1 (significantly) then either the claim is an overstatement, far fewer people are dying of other causes (i.e. corona cures cancer, heart disease...), or somewhere in between.

Using official UK total data, T-1 is actually zero for all months in 2020 except April where it was around 0.75, so I don't even have to bother looking up corona data to know that all present claims of corona deaths are either overstated or that corona somehow cured the person of other morbidities.
